text: Hi, my name is Bread. I'm a big coffee lover, so I guess I'll start there. I can't really start my day without a cup of coffee, and this morning was no different. I had one before I came to take this test, and I'm already looking forward to another one once it's over. I work in IT at Samsung Heavy Industries. I'm in charge of our IT systems, so my days are pretty busy. I live in an apartment with my wife, and we're pretty much homebodies. In my free time, I like listening to music, playing computer games, and reading. So, yeah, that's me in a nutshell: coffee, my wife, and my computer. I'm happy to be here, and I hope I do well today!

Recycling is a big deal in Korea. We take it very seriously. Almost everyone sorts their trash into paper, plastic, glass, cans, and food waste. Each apartment complex has a recycling area, and there are separate bins for each type. We have to rinse the containers and take off the labels, otherwise it's a pain for the workers. Food waste is a separate system, too. In many places, you have to pay for a special trash bag for general waste, so people try to throw away less. It was a hassle at first, but now it's second nature. I think it's a good habit, especially for a country with limited space.

I don't recycle every day, but we collect things all week. Here's how it works. First, we separate everything in the kitchen: plastic bottles, cans, paper, and so on. Second, we rinse the containers, and my wife is very strict about this. Third, we remove the labels and flatten the boxes to save space. Then, we put everything into separate bags. Once a week, usually on Wednesday evening, I carry the bags down to the recycling area in our apartment complex. I sort them into the right bins, and food waste goes into a special machine with a card. It's a short trip, but it's become part of my weekly routine. And I usually grab a coffee on my way back!

One time, I had a funny, and a little stressful, experience. I had just bought a pair of wireless earbuds, and I was cleaning up all the boxes and packaging. I put everything in a big bag and took it down to the recycling area. When I got back, I couldn't find my earbuds! I looked everywhere in the house. Then it hit me: I must have thrown them away with the box! I ran back downstairs. It was already dark, and the bins were full. So there I was, using my phone as a flashlight, digging through a pile of cardboard boxes. A neighbor walked by and gave me a very strange look. I just smiled and said, "I'm looking for something." Finally, after about 20 minutes, I found it! My wife couldn't stop laughing when I came back, covered in dust. Since then, I always check the box twice before I throw it away.

We have quite a few holidays in Korea. The two biggest ones are Seollal, which is Lunar New Year, and Chuseok. On Seollal, we wear traditional clothes, called hanbok, and bow to our elders to wish them a happy new year. We eat rice cake soup, and kids get pocket money. Chuseok is more like Thanksgiving. We visit our hometowns and share a big meal with family. Besides those, there's Children's Day in May, Buddha's Birthday, and Hangul Day, which celebrates our alphabet. And of course, Christmas is a holiday, too, but it's more of a couples' day. On most holidays, people take time off, spend time with family, and eat a lot of food.

When I was a kid, my favorite holiday was Seollal. I spent it with my parents and my six older sisters at our little house with the yard. The whole house was packed, and it was chaos in the best way. In the morning, we all put on our hanbok, and I had to bow to my parents and my relatives. I hated it at first, but then they gave me pocket money! I counted it every year. We ate rice cake soup, and my sisters and I played yut, a traditional board game, on the floor. Of course, my sisters always cheated, and I always cried. But we always ended up laughing. Looking back, those were the best days. I miss that noisy house.

The last holiday I had was Chuseok, just a couple of weeks ago. We spent the first day at my father-in-law's house with the whole family. After that, we had a few days off, so we took it easy. What made this holiday special was that I really got to rest. As an IT manager, my phone usually rings on holidays, and I have to deal with problems. But this time, nothing happened. I turned off my work notifications, and my phone was quiet for the whole holiday. We slept in, went for a walk at Deokpo Beach, and had coffee while watching the waves. My daughter Eunbin even cooked for us! It was simple, but it was exactly what I needed. I felt completely recharged.

My favorite kind of movie is sci-fi. I love movies about space, time travel, and the future. I think I like them because of my job. I work with technology every day, so it's fun to imagine where it could go. Sci-fi movies make me think, like "What if this really happened?" I also love the visual effects. Seeing a spaceship fly across the screen is amazing, especially in a big theater. They're a great way to escape from reality, and I can forget about work stress for two hours. I also like action movies, but sci-fi is my number one. My wife prefers romantic comedies, so we usually take turns choosing.

The last time I went to a movie was about a month ago. I went with my son, Suhyun. It was a sci-fi action movie, of course. Before the movie, we grabbed a quick dinner: burgers and fries. Then we got popcorn and drinks, and I got a large coffee, which I regretted later because I had to go to the bathroom in the middle of the movie! The movie itself was exciting, with lots of explosions. Suhyun was on the edge of his seat the whole time. After the movie, we walked around for a bit and talked about our favorite scenes. He kept saying, "That part was so cool!" It was a great father-and-son night out.

The most memorable movie for me is "Interstellar." It's about a father who travels through space to save humanity, but he has to leave his kids behind. The story is amazing, and the music is incredible. I watched it in a theater a long time ago, and I felt so many emotions. The space scenes were breathtaking. But the most emotional part is the father and his daughter. There's a scene where he watches video messages from his kids, who have grown up while he was away. I started crying, and I'm not a person who cries easily. Now that I'm a father myself, it hits even harder. It made me think about how precious time with family is.

Hey, it's me. I've been thinking about going to the beach this weekend. Are you in?. Great! First, which beach do you want to go to? I was thinking Deokpo, but I'm open to other ideas.. Okay. What time should we leave? I'd like to avoid the traffic.. Sounds good. Who's driving? I can drive if you want.. One last thing: what should we bring? Towels, sunscreen, and snacks?. I'll bring the coffee, of course! This is going to be fun. See you soon!

Hey, it's me. I have some bad news. I just checked the weather forecast, and a typhoon is coming this weekend. They say there'll be heavy rain and strong winds, so it's not safe to go to the beach. I'm really bummed, because I was looking forward to it. But I have a few ideas. First, we could postpone the trip until next weekend, when the weather should be better. Or, if you'd rather do something this weekend, we could go to an aquarium, which is indoors. And if you don't feel like going out at all, we could have a movie night at my place, and I'll make coffee. What do you think?

Yes, I had a painful experience at Deokpo Beach last summer. My wife and I went for a swim in the evening. The water was calm, and I was floating on my back, enjoying the view. Suddenly, I felt a sharp pain on my arm, like an electric shock! I looked down and saw a jellyfish. I panicked and swam back to the shore as fast as I could. My arm was red and swollen, and it hurt like crazy. A lifeguard saw me and came over right away. He rinsed my arm with seawater, not fresh water, and used a card to scrape off the stingers. He told me to go to the hospital just in case. I went, and they gave me some cream. Luckily, I was fine in a couple of days. Since then, I always check for jellyfish warnings, and I stay close to the shore. My wife still teases me about it.

When something goes wrong at home, I usually start by searching online. YouTube is my best friend. If a faucet leaks or a light switch breaks, I watch a tutorial and try to fix it myself. If it's too complicated, I use an app to call a repairman. And for big problems, I call my father-in-law, since he's so good with his hands. My parents did things very differently. They didn't have smartphones, so they relied on experience. My dad would grab his toolbox and fix things on his own. If he couldn't, he'd ask the neighbors, and someone always knew what to do. Today, I don't know my neighbors very well, so I just search online. I think the old way was warmer, but the new way is definitely faster.

Renting a place can be stressful, and people worry about a lot of things. The biggest concern in Korea is the deposit. We often pay a huge deposit, and people are afraid of losing it if the landlord can't pay it back. There are also scams, so people have to be careful. Other common concerns are the rent being too high, the condition of the place, and noisy neighbors. How do people deal with these problems? They usually check the building's records online to make sure the landlord really owns it. They also go through a real estate agent, visit the place in person, and read the contract carefully. Some people buy deposit insurance. In my case, being in IT, I'd check everything twice. My advice is: don't rush, and always ask questions.
